title: Optimal Subgroup Discovery at Every Support Threshold
claim: Ranking subgroups by support-weighted divergence is unreliable at small sample sizes, because estimation noise lets spurious groups outscore true ones.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: densities, score vs sample size with bands, error rate curve
description: Three side-by-side line plots with legends above the first two. Left: density curves over a value axis from about -4 to 4. A green dotted curve shows a 5-mode Gaussian mixture background, which is also Subgroup B (spurious). A purple dashed curve shows Subgroup A (true), with taller peaks at the outer modes and at the center. Middle: support-weighted KL estimate against Subgroup A sample size k, from 10 to 100. The purple line for A stays near 0.025–0.03 and the green dashed line for B falls from about 0.038 to under 0.01. Shaded 95% bands overlap heavily at small k. Right: a red line with diamond markers shows the ranking error rate falling from about 63% at k=10 to near 0% at k=100. The purple and green pairing is used consistently, and the eye goes to the overlapping bands and the steep red curve.
caption: Ranking error under support-weighted KL estimation with finite samples. Two subgroups are drawn from a 5-mode Gaussian mixture background: Subgroup A (true, support = 0.08, KL ≈ 0.25) and Subgroup B (spurious, support = 0.15, KL = 0). Left: Conditional densities of the subgroups and background. Middle: Support-weighted KL estimates (support × KL) as a function of Subgroup A’s sample size k, with B’s size scaled by the support ratio; shaded regions show the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range over 300 draws. At small k, estimation noise inflates B’s score above A’s despite its zero true divergence. Right: Fraction of trials in which the spurious Subgroup B is ranked above the true Subgroup A. At k = 30 the error rate still exceeds 20%, showing that support-weighted KL ranking is unreliable at small sample sizes.
abstract: Subgroup discovery aims to identify regions of the feature space where a target variable deviates from its marginal distribution. A fundamental challenge in this problem is the trade-off between a subgroup's deviation and its support: small subgroups can be highly deviating but statistically meaningless, while large ones cannot deviate much by construction. Existing methods tackle this challenge by collapsing the two into a single scalar quality measure, implicitly committing to one particular trade-off and making it difficult to recover the most deviating subgroup under a user-specified support constraint. We instead provide the first theoretical and structural characterization of optimal subgroups with maximum Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence under arbitrary support constraints. Under a partition-based generative model, where the feature space decomposes into regions of homogeneous conditional distributions of the target variable called atoms, we prove that every point on the deviation-support Pareto front is a union of whole atoms together with at most one fractional atom. This reduces an uncountable search to a finite combinatorial problem. Guided by this theory, we propose a simple two-step recipe: learn a homogeneous partition, then select atoms greedily. Across 19 benchmark datasets, it finds the most deviating subgroups at a range of support thresholds, and reliably improves subgroups returned by existing methods when applied as a post-processing step. These results empirically validate the sufficiency and necessity of our theoretical contributions.
